stimuli.text: Researchers grew a population of flour beetles in a container with a fixed supply of resources and counted the population every two days.

questions.stem: A PCR reaction starts with 10 copyies of a target DNA sequence. Assuming each cycle doubles the DNA, how many copies are present after 6 cycles?

options.why: Correct. Each cycle doubles the number of copies.
There are 6 doublings.
Copies double each cycle; they do not increase by 2.
Growth is exponential with base 2.

questions.explanation: After 6 doublings: 10 × 2^6 copies.

questions.stem: A circular plasmid of 4000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1300 and 3000. The fragments are separated by gel electrophoresis. Which bands appear, and which travels farthest?

options.text: 1700 bp and 2300 bp; the 2300 bp band travels farthest
options.why: Smaller fragments move through the gel more easily.

options.text: 1700 bp and 2300 bp; the 1700 bp band travels farthest
options.why: Correct. Two cuts in a circle give two pieces; smaller fragments move farther.

options.text: 1300 bp, 1700 bp and 1000 bp; the 1000 bp band travels farthest
options.why: A circular plasmid cut twice gives two fragments, not three.
The plasmid is cut into pieces.

questions.explanation: The fragments are 3000 − 1300 = 1700 bp and 4000 − 1700 = 2300 bp.

questions.stem: 114 amino acids are joined into one linear polypeptide by dehydration synthesis. How many water molecules are released?

options.why: Correct. A chain of 114 monomers has 113 bonds, and each bond involves one water molecule.
There is one fewer bond than monomers in a linear chain.
There is one fewer bond than monomers.
Each bond involves one water molecule, not two.

questions.explanation: Linking 114 monomers forms 113 bonds; each releases one water molecule.

questions.stem: Cyanide blocks the final protein of the electron transport chain in mitochondria. Which is the most immediate effect?

options.text: The proton gradient is no longer maintained, so ATP synthase makes much less ATP
options.why: Correct. Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so pumping stops.
Glycolysis can continue briefly.
Oxygen is no longer reduced.
ATP production falls.

questions.explanation: Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so pumping stops.

questions.stem: How does a phosphorylation cascade amplify a signal?

options.why: Phosphatases remove them.
It produces a response, not ligand.

options.text: Each activated kinase activates many molecules at the next step
options.why: Correct. Each step multiplies the number of active molecules.
One ligand binds one receptor.

questions.explanation: Each step multiplies the number of active molecules.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 21% guanine. What percentage of the bases are adenine?

options.why: 21% is the amount of cytosine, which pairs with guanine.
Correct. cytosine also makes up 21%; the remaining 58% is split equally between the other two bases.
That is the total for both remaining bases together.
Both members of each base pair must be accounted for.

questions.explanation: By base pairing, guanine = cytosine = 21%. The other two bases share 58%, so each is 29%.

questions.stem: Two cube-shaped cells have side lengths of 4 µm and 8 µm. Which statement correctly compares their surface area-to-volume ratios?

options.text: The 4 µm cell has a ratio of 1.5, which is greater than the 8 µm cell's 0.75, so it exchanges materials more efficiently
options.why: Correct. For a cube, SA:V = 6s²/s³ = 6/s.

options.text: Both cells have the same ratio, 6, because both are cubes
options.why: The ratio depends on side length.

options.text: The 4 µm cell has a ratio of 1.5, which is greater, so it exchanges materials less efficiently
options.why: A greater ratio means more surface per unit volume: more efficient exchange.

options.text: The 8 µm cell has the greater ratio, 48, so it exchanges materials more efficiently
options.why: SA:V decreases as size increases.

questions.explanation: SA:V = 6/s: 1.5 for 4 µm and 0.75 for 8 µm. Smaller cells have more surface area per unit volume.

questions.stem: Why can cells divide uncontrollably when a gene for a growth-factor receptor is mutated so the receptor is always active?

options.why: It is always active.
It divides instead.

options.text: The cell can no longer replicate DNA
options.why: Replication still occurs.

options.text: The cell behaves as if it is always receiving signals to divide
options.why: Correct. A constitutively active receptor drives division without the signal.

questions.explanation: A constitutively active receptor drives division without the signal.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 22% thymine. What percentage of the bases are guanine?

questions.stem: A diploid cell has 46 chromosomes (2n = 46). How many chromatids are present in the cell during G2?

questions.stem: Breeders produced broccoli, kale and cabbage from wild mustard. How does this differ from natural selection?

options.text: Mutation did not occur in any plants
options.why: Variation came from mutations.
Correct. That is artificial selection.
They were heritable.
Variation was essential.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA reads 5′-GAAAGTCT-3′. What is the sequence of the complementary strand, written 5′ to 3′?

The complementary strand is antiparallel; written 5′ to 3′ it is reversed.

questions.stem: Which feature allows carbon to form the backbone of diverse biological molecules?

options.text: It is the most abundant element in water
options.why: Water contains no carbon.

options.text: It forms ionic bonds with hydrogen
options.why: Carbon–hydrogen bonds are covalent.

options.text: It can form four covalent bonds, building chains, branches and rings
options.why: Correct. Carbon's bonding versatility allows many structures.
Carbon readily bonds with oxygen.

questions.explanation: Carbon's bonding versatility allows many structures.

questions.stem: The producers in an ecosystem store 10,000 kcal of energy. Assuming about 10% transfer between trophic levels, about how much energy is available to the tertiary consumers?

options.why: Count the number of transfers from producers.
About 10% is passed on; about 90% is lost.
Correct. 3 transfers of 10% each.
Count the number of transfers from producers.

questions.explanation: Each level keeps about 10%: 10,000 × 0.1^3 = 10 kcal.

questions.stem: A mutation causes a G protein to remain permanently active. What is the most likely effect?

options.why: Binding is upstream of the G protein.
That is unrelated.

questions.explanation: Downstream steps stay switched on.

questions.stem: An antibiotic is used to treat an infection, and resistant bacteria become common. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Resistant bacteria were present before treatment and survived to reproduce
options.why: Correct. The antibiotic selected existing variants.

options.text: The antibiotic caused the mutations for resistance
options.why: Mutations arise randomly.

options.why: Individuals do not adapt this way.

options.why: Resistance spreads through bacterial reproduction and gene transfer.

questions.explanation: The antibiotic selected existing variants.

questions.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 16. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can it produce by independent assortment?

questions.stem: How does an enzyme speed up a reaction?

parts.prompt: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable in the experiment, and identify one variable that should be held constant.

parts.prompt: The student repeats the experiment at pH 6 with twice as much enzyme and the same amount of substrate. Predict the effect on the initial rate, and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Predicts the initial rate increases.
rubric.example: Higher than 51 µmol/min, up to about double.

rubric.criterion: Justifies with more active sites available when substrate is plentiful.
rubric.example: More enzyme molecules can bind substrate at the same time.

parts.prompt: A competitive inhibitor is added to the reaction at the optimal pH. Describe how increasing the substrate concentration would affect the inhibition, and explain why.

rubric.criterion: Inhibition decreases at high substrate concentration.
rubric.example: The rate approaches the uninhibited maximum.

rubric.criterion: Explains competition for the active site.
rubric.example: Substrate molecules outcompete the inhibitor for the active site.

parts.prompt: Describe how you would construct an appropriate graph of the data: the type of graph, the axes and their labels, and the scale.

rubric.criterion: Line or scatter graph with time on the x-axis.
rubric.example: Day on the x-axis, population size on the y-axis.

rubric.criterion: Axes labeled with units and linear scales; points plotted accurately and connected.
rubric.example: y-axis from 0 to at least 600.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of population growth between day 8 and day 12.

rubric.criterion: Correct calculation with units.
rubric.example: (599 − 580) ÷ 4 = 4.75 individuals per day

parts.prompt: Identify the type of population growth shown and estimate the carrying capacity.

rubric.criterion: Logistic growth.
rubric.example: An S-shaped curve that levels off.

rubric.criterion: Carrying capacity estimate consistent with the data.
rubric.example: About 600.

parts.prompt: Explain why the growth rate decreases as the population approaches the carrying capacity.

rubric.criterion: Identifies a density-dependent factor.
rubric.example: Competition for limited food and space, or buildup of wastes.

rubric.criterion: Links it to lower birth rates or higher death rates.
rubric.example: As density rises, fewer resources per individual reduce reproduction and survival.

parts.prompt: The researchers repeat the experiment with double the food supply. Predict the effect on the carrying capacity and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Predicts a higher carrying capacity.
rubric.example: Greater than about 600.

rubric.criterion: Justifies: food was a limiting resource.
rubric.example: More resources allow the environment to support more individuals.

parts.prompt: Identify an appropriate control for the experiment, and explain why the students measured percent change rather than change in mass.

rubric.criterion: The 0 M (distilled water) treatment, or cores with no solution change.
rubric.example: Distilled water.

rubric.criterion: Percent change allows comparison of cores with slightly different starting masses.
rubric.example: It standardizes for initial mass.

parts.prompt: Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic to the potato cells, and calculate the solute potential of that solution (Ψs = −iCRT, R = 0.0831, T in kelvins).

rubric.criterion: Isotonic concentration where the change in mass is zero.
rubric.example: About 0.3 M, interpolating between 0.2 and 0.4 M.

rubric.criterion: Solute potential calculated correctly from the estimate.

parts.prompt: Explain the change in mass of the cores in the 0.8 M solution.

rubric.criterion: Water moved out of the cells by osmosis toward the lower water potential of the solution.
rubric.example: The solution is hypertonic, so the cells lost water and mass.

parts.prompt: Describe the role of cAMP in this pathway.

rubric.criterion: cAMP is a second messenger that relays and amplifies the signal inside the cell.
rubric.example: It activates protein kinase A.

parts.prompt: Explain how a single epinephrine molecule can cause the release of a large number of glucose molecules.

rubric.criterion: Amplification: each activated enzyme activates many molecules at the next step.
rubric.example: One adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP; each kinase phosphorylates many targets.

parts.prompt: A mutation alters adenylyl cyclase, so that it cannot make cAMP. Predict the effect on glycogen breakdown, and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Correct prediction.
rubric.example: Glycogen is not broken down in response to epinephrine.

rubric.criterion: Justification using the pathway.
rubric.example: Without the second messenger, protein kinase A is not activated.

parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the b allele and the expected number of heterozygous beetles.

rubric.criterion: q from the recessive phenotype frequency.
Expected heterozygotes.

parts.prompt: Identify two conditions that must be met for the population to remain in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.

rubric.criterion: Two correct conditions.
rubric.example: A large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no natural selection.

parts.prompt: Birds that prey on the beetles find beetles with green shells more easily on the new background. Predict how the frequency of the b allele will change over several generations, and justify your prediction.

rubric.criterion: Predicts q increases.
rubric.example: Beetles with brown shells (bb) survive and reproduce more.

rubric.criterion: Justifies with differential survival and reproduction.
rubric.example: Selection removes B alleles faster, because both BB and Bb beetles are eaten more.

parts.prompt: State the null hypothesis, and calculate the expected number of offspring in each category.

rubric.criterion: Null hypothesis: the genes assort independently, giving a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio.
rubric.example: Any differences are due to chance.

rubric.criterion: Expected counts.

parts.prompt: Calculate the chi-square value and determine whether to reject the null hypothesis at p = 0.05 (critical value 7.81 for 3 degrees of freedom).

rubric.criterion: Correct chi-square value.
Correct conclusion with comparison to the critical value.
rubric.example: 0.24 is less than 7.81, so fail to reject the null hypothesis.

parts.prompt: Propose an explanation for the results.

rubric.criterion: Explanation consistent with the conclusion.
rubric.example: The genes assort independently; deviations are due to chance.
